text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- SAFETY-CRITICAL: do not continue repeated summer peak-load testing until the shutdown cause is verified. A generator that stalls hot under load can create transfer-switch instability, nuisance outages, and in the wrong setting can expose connected equipment to undervoltage/frequency collapse just before shutdown. If this unit serves life-safety, medical, telecom, or fire protection loads, place it in restricted service until a loaded verification test is completed.
- Root cause most likely: heat-related fuel delivery or fuel shutoff control failure, with ECU-1425 strongly suggesting an ECU-detected protective or control-side fault rather than a purely mechanical engine seizure. On a 2016 Cummins RS20A generator that runs normally for about 15 minutes, then stalls only under load and restarts after a 30-minute cool-down, the pattern fits a component that degrades with temperature: fuel solenoid coil, lift pump, fuel pump driver/control circuit, or a temperature-sensitive sensor/input that causes the controller to command shutdown.
- Code interpretation: ECU-1425 is the only fault text provided, and because no auto-detected code family was captured, the exact wording must be confirmed from the controller event log. On Cummins/PowerCommand-family equipment, “ECU” faults often indicate an engine control module-reported issue rather than a simple operator panel alarm. The fact that the code is tied to a hot, loaded stall makes it diagnostically important even without a full SPN/FMI-style translation. The shop must pull the complete event history from the genset controller and engine ECU, not just the front-panel display.
- Component failure analysis: the strongest real-world pattern here is a fuel system component that works cold, then opens electrically or loses output as winding temperature rises. A weak fuel shutoff solenoid can drop out once hot and recover after cooling. A marginal electric lift pump can also lose pressure after 10–20 minutes under sustained load, especially in summer ambient conditions when fuel temperature rises. Because you already confirmed oil level is correct and cooling vents are clear, the usual simple shutdown causes are less likely, but coolant temperature, intake air temperature, and controller heat-soak still must be measured rather than assumed.
- Load-specific behavior matters: “runs 15 minutes then stalls under load” is more consistent with fuel starvation, thermal derate/shutdown, or an electrical control dropout than with a no-load idle issue. If it were a clogged vent or severe fuel restriction, the recent fuel filter change helps but does not rule out algae, tank pickup restriction, collapsing hose liner, or a blocked tank vent. “Changed last season” is not the same as “verified clean under current summer load.”
- Age considerations: a 2016 unit is old enough for heat-cycled relays, solenoids, harness connectors, and pump motors to become intermittent even if total hours are unknown. The missing hour data lowers certainty because generator failures are driven more by hours, load profile, and maintenance intervals than by calendar age alone.
- Confidence: 74%.
- More data is required before authorizing parts replacement.
- Data Needed
- Pull the exact ECU-1425 description from the controller/ECM event log, including active/inactive status, occurrence count, and timestamp relative to the stall.
- Record coolant temperature, oil pressure, battery voltage, frequency, and fuel pressure from cold start through the 15-minute loaded stall event.
- Measure fuel supply pressure/vacuum before and after the filter during the failure, not just at idle.
- Verify whether the engine dies abruptly like key-off/fuel-solenoid dropout or sags/surges first like fuel starvation.
- Provide photos of the controller model, engine data plate, fuel system layout, and any shutdown/alarm screen immediately after the event.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Most likely alternative: hot-failing fuel shutoff solenoid or run relay. This is ruled in by the clean restart after a 30-minute cool-down and the abrupt nature many operators describe as “stalls.” It is ruled out if fuel pressure remains stable and the solenoid stays energized during the event.
- Second likely alternative: weak electric lift pump or restricted fuel supply path. This fits a generator that carries load for a short period, then starves as demand and fuel temperature rise. It is ruled in if pressure drops progressively before shutdown or if clear return-line aeration is seen. It is ruled out if pressure remains within spec at the moment of stall.
- Third likely alternative: thermal shutdown from coolant temperature, intake restriction, or radiator performance degradation. Even with vents clear, internal radiator fouling, slipping fan drive, weak water pump flow, or a bad coolant temp sensor can trigger shutdown during summer peak tests. It is ruled in if coolant temperature climbs abnormally or if the controller logs high engine temp before stall.
- Fourth likely alternative: controller/ECU heat-soak or failing sensor input. A crank sensor, cam sensor, or ECU power supply issue can open when hot and recover after cooling. This is common on aging industrial equipment where vibration and heat harden insulation. It is ruled in if RPM signal drops out instantly on the data log while fuel pressure remains normal.
- Fifth likely alternative: tank vent restriction or pickup tube issue. A blocked vent can create vacuum in the tank during sustained draw, especially under summer heat. It is ruled in if the unit runs longer with the cap/vent path temporarily corrected or if supply vacuum rises steadily during the test.
- Less likely: alternator/load-side electrical fault causing engine overload. If the generator end develops abnormal drag or the connected test bank/site load is excessive or unbalanced, the engine may bog and stall. This is less likely because the cool-down restart pattern points more strongly to heat-sensitive control/fuel issues, but it must be checked by comparing behavior on a known-good load bank.
- Less likely: old fuel, microbial contamination, or water in fuel. A filter changed last season does not eliminate contaminated fuel. This is ruled in if a sample shows water, dark biological debris, or if differential restriction across the filter rises under load.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- The shop must perform a controlled loaded run with live data capture. Use the Cummins service tool appropriate to the controller/engine package, plus a calibrated load bank if site load is inconsistent. Record coolant temp, oil pressure, battery voltage, engine speed, frequency, and any active shutdown reason from cold start until failure. Expected result: one parameter should clearly deviate just before stall rather than guessing after the fact. Typical diagnostic cost: $180–$450 depending on travel and load-bank setup.
- Install a fuel pressure gauge and, if possible, a vacuum gauge on the supply side. Measure cold pressure, hot pressure at 10 minutes, and pressure at the exact stall point. Expected result: pressure should remain stable under load; a drop just before shutdown strongly supports lift pump restriction or suction-side blockage. Typical cost: $120–$250 if done during the same diagnostic session.
- Check fuel shutoff solenoid voltage and coil resistance cold versus hot. Use a DVOM and amp clamp; monitor whether the solenoid loses command voltage or opens internally when heat-soaked. Expected result: command voltage should remain steady; if voltage stays present but the solenoid drops out hot, the solenoid is defective. Typical cost: $80–$180 incremental.
- Verify cooling system performance with infrared thermometer and, ideally, live ECU temperature data. Compare thermostat housing, upper/lower radiator tank temperatures, and fan airflow under load. Expected result: a normal temperature spread and no runaway climb. If the controller logs overtemp while the engine is not truly overheating, suspect sensor or wiring error. Typical cost: $90–$200.
- Inspect and heat-stress critical relays, ECU power feeds, and engine speed sensor circuits. Use a heat gun carefully on suspect relays/connectors after baseline testing, and wiggle-test harnesses near the engine. Expected result: reproducing the stall electrically is strong proof of an intermittent control fault. Typical cost: $120–$300.
- If the shop cannot reproduce the fault on load, they have not completed the diagnosis. A no-load idle test is not sufficient for your symptom set.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- “What is the exact text definition of ECU-1425 on this RS20A, and can you print the event log showing whether it is active or stored?” They must show the controller/ECM report, not just say “it had a code.”
- “What were fuel pressure and supply vacuum readings cold, at 10 minutes, and at the moment of stall under load?” If they have no numbers, they did not test the most likely branch.
- “Did the engine die abruptly like fuel shutoff loss, or did RPM/frequency sag first like fuel starvation?” A competent shop will describe the failure signature clearly.
- “What was coolant temperature from startup to shutdown, and did the controller log a high-temp or sensor plausibility event?” They should provide actual values, not “it didn’t seem hot.”
- “Did you test it on a known load bank or only observe it on site load?” If they only guessed from building load behavior, the diagnosis is incomplete.
- Red flags to watch for:
- “We’ll start with filter, pump, sensor, and solenoid and see what fixes it.” That is a parts cannon, not diagnosis.
- “No codes means no electrical issue.” False. Heat-related electrical failures often leave intermittent or non-latched events.
- “The vents are clear, so it can’t be overheating.” External vent condition does not prove internal cooling performance.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve done some research and want to understand what testing shows on this Cummins RS20A, especially because it only stalls after about 15 minutes under summer load.”
- Phrasing: keep it curious and specific. “Help me understand how you ruled out hot fuel starvation versus a thermal shutdown or solenoid dropout.”
- Example dialogue: “Can you show me the exact ECU-1425 definition from the controller and whether it occurred at the same time as the stall?”
- Example dialogue: “What were the fuel pressure readings during the loaded run, not just at startup?”
- Example dialogue: “Did RPM and frequency fall gradually before shutdown, or did it stop abruptly like the fuel command was lost?”
- Example dialogue: “What coolant temperature did you record at the thermostat housing and in the ECU data when it failed?”
- Example dialogue: “If you’re recommending a pump or solenoid, what test result specifically condemned that part?”
- Body language: bring a notebook, pause after answers, and ask for printouts calmly. A professional, unhurried tone gets better data than sounding suspicious.
- Response handling if they get defensive: “I’m not questioning your experience. I just authorize generator repairs based on measured values because intermittent hot faults can get expensive fast.”
- Response handling if they stay vague: “I’d be more comfortable approving diagnosis time for a loaded data capture than approving parts without failure-point readings.”
- Exit strategy: “Please email me the event log, the line-item quote, and the readings you captured during the stall. I’d like to review those before authorizing parts.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Fair diagnostic pricing:
- Loaded diagnostic session with event-log retrieval and basic electrical checks: $180–$450.
- Fuel pressure/vacuum instrumentation during loaded run: add $120–$250.
- Cooling system thermal verification and sensor plausibility checks: add $90–$200.
- Fair repair ranges if diagnosis confirms the fault:
- Fuel shutoff solenoid or run relay repair: typically $180–$550 depending on access and whether OEM control parts are used.
- Electric lift pump replacement: commonly $350–$900 installed depending on exact engine package and mounting location.
- Coolant temperature sensor or wiring repair: commonly $220–$650 installed.
- Harness/connector repair for heat-damaged wiring: commonly $200–$800 depending on extent.
- If multiple maintenance items are proposed, insist on separation between “fault repair” and “preventive service.” A fuel filter, coolant flush, and battery service may be reasonable maintenance, but they should not be bundled as if they prove the stall cause.
- Overcharge markers:
- Charging several hours of diagnosis without a loaded reproduction or data log.
- Replacing pump, solenoid, and sensors together without readings.
- Billing premium “generator emergency” rates for a non-emergency shop visit without after-hours dispatch.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts cannon indicator: the shop recommends fuel filter, lift pump, shutoff solenoid, and temp sensor all at once because “one of them is probably it.” That transfers diagnostic risk to you.
- Diagnostic shortcut: they run it unloaded for five minutes, declare it fine, then recommend generic tune-up parts. Your symptom occurs under summer load after 15 minutes; anything less is not representative testing.
- Price gouging red flag: a basic relay or solenoid billed at several times dealer/OEM pricing without justification, or a “controller reset/programming” charge when no software issue has been proven.
- Another shortcut: relying only on the front-panel alarm history and never connecting to the engine/controller service tool. ECU-1425 must be decoded properly.
- Another gouging sign: charging load-bank rental when they never actually document kilowatt load, frequency, and failure time.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately:
- One proper loaded diagnostic session with event-log retrieval and live data capture.
- Fuel pressure/vacuum testing during the failure window.
- Cooling system temperature verification with ECU data comparison.
- Reject outright:
- Blind replacement of multiple fuel and electrical parts without failure-point measurements.
- Generic “summer service” packages sold as the cure for a hot stall.
- Any recommendation to keep running repeated peak tests “until it gets worse.”
- Get a second opinion when:
- The shop cannot define ECU-1425 exactly.
- They refuse to provide readings from the loaded test.
- Their recommendation changes from visit to visit without new data.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: your RS20A must maintain stable engine speed to hold generator frequency under load. As load increases, the engine control system commands more fuel while monitoring temperature, oil pressure, and speed. If fuel delivery weakens or a protective input trips, the controller shuts the engine down to prevent damage.
- Failure mechanism for hot fuel issues: electric pumps and solenoids contain windings that can open or lose strength as temperature rises. A component may pass a cold ohms test and still fail after 10–20 minutes of real load. That is why loaded hot testing matters more than static checks.
- Failure mechanism for thermal shutdowns: even with clear exterior vents, radiator cores can be internally restricted, fins can be packed with debris, fan performance can drop, or a sensor can misreport temperature. Summer peak tests expose these weaknesses because ambient temperature and load are both high.
- Why cool-down restart matters: a 30-minute recovery window is classic for heat-soak electrical faults and some fuel starvation conditions. Mechanical failures usually do not recover that neatly.
- Prevention tips:
- Exercise the generator monthly under meaningful load, not just idle/no-load, so weak hot components show up before peak season.
- Replace fuel filters by hours/calendar and sample fuel annually for water and microbial growth.
- Record shutdown codes, ambient temperature, load percentage, and run time every time a fault occurs. Pattern data is extremely valuable on standby equipment.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Specific part numbers cannot be responsibly given from the data provided because RS20A configurations vary by engine build, controller, and serial number. Cummins/Onan parts are serial-number sensitive, and ordering by model alone risks the wrong pump, sensor, or solenoid.
- Why OEM matters here:
- Fuel shutoff solenoids and control relays must match pull-in/hold characteristics and connector quality; aftermarket mismatches can create repeat hot-stall complaints.
- Temperature sensors and engine speed sensors must report correct values to the controller; cheap substitutes can create false shutdowns.
- Generator applications are less tolerant of marginal parts than automotive use because frequency stability and automatic transfer operation depend on precise control.
- Best sourcing strategy:
- Use Cummins QuickServe Online and a Cummins distributor/dealer parts desk with the full model and serial number.
- Ask the shop to provide the exact Cummins part number from the serial-number lookup before you approve anything.
- If they propose aftermarket parts, ask for the OEM number they cross from and the warranty terms in writing.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Ask for a line-item estimate separating diagnosis, parts, labor, travel, and load-bank charges. Generator invoices get inflated when everything is buried in one lump sum.
- Use measured-value leverage: “If fuel pressure stayed in spec at stall, I don’t want to pay for a pump. If the solenoid lost hold hot, I’ll approve that repair.” This keeps the conversation evidence-based.
- Ask labor justification questions: “What is the access time for this component on this enclosure, and how much of that overlaps with the diagnostic setup already performed?”
- Compare OEM parts pricing through a Cummins distributor before approving. Even if you buy through the shop, knowing list price prevents excessive markup.
- Walk-away points:
- No exact definition of ECU-1425.
- No loaded reproduction of the fault.
- Recommendation for multiple parts without readings.
- Strong leverage statement: “I’m ready to approve the repair that your test results actually support today.”

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: hot-failing fuel delivery/control component — 74% confidence. The 15-minute loaded run, summer-only pattern, and 30-minute cool-down restart strongly fit a lift pump, fuel shutoff solenoid, or related control circuit that degrades with heat.
- Secondary cause: thermal shutdown or false overtemperature input — 16% confidence. Summer peak tests make this plausible, and clear vents do not rule out radiator inefficiency or a bad temp sensor, but the restart-after-cooling pattern still overlaps with the primary branch.
- Tertiary cause: hot intermittent ECU/sensor/power-feed fault — 10% confidence. ECU-1425 keeps this in play, especially if RPM signal or controller power drops abruptly, but without the exact code definition it remains behind the fuel branch.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions required:
- Stop nonessential peak-load testing until a loaded diagnostic session is completed.
- Capture the exact ECU-1425 definition and event history before any codes are cleared.
- Schedule a test under controlled load with fuel pressure, temperature, and voltage monitored through the failure window.
- Future maintenance schedule:
- Monthly exercise under at least a meaningful building/load-bank load per site requirements, with run time and temperatures logged.
- Annual fuel quality check and tank vent inspection, especially before summer season.
- Cooling system inspection before peak season, including radiator cleanliness, coolant condition, hose integrity, and fan performance.
- Warning signs to monitor:
- Frequency droop, hunting, or surging before shutdown.
- Abrupt stop as if key-off, which points more toward solenoid/control loss.
- Any recurrence tied specifically to high ambient temperature or higher-than-normal load percentage.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Cummins QuickServe Online service portal: https://quickserve.cummins.com/ — authoritative Cummins source for serial-number-specific fault code definitions, wiring diagrams, and troubleshooting trees. This is the correct OEM resource to decode ECU-1425 on your exact genset/engine combination.
- Cummins PowerCommand generator set operator and service literature portal: https://www.cummins.com/generators/manuals — direct OEM manuals source for controller alarm handling, shutdown logic, and maintenance procedures relevant to RS-series standby generators.
- Smokstak Onan/Cummins generator forum: https://www.smokstak.com/forum/forums/onan-generator-forum.1/ — independent technician/owner archive with many real-world hot-stall, fuel-solenoid, and lift-pump failure cases on Cummins/Onan standby units. Use it for pattern confirmation, not as a substitute for OEM test procedures.
- Because the exact serial number and controller variant were not provided, no responsible technician should cite a serial-specific Cummins bulletin number as definitively applicable yet. The next step is to pull the exact QuickServe documentation for your unit.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize one proper loaded diagnostic session that captures the exact ECU-1425 definition, fuel pressure, coolant temperature, and shutdown data at the moment it stalls.
- Do not approve any pump, solenoid, sensor, or controller parts until the shop shows measured readings proving which branch failed hot.
- Get the model/serial/controller information and use Cummins QuickServe or a Cummins distributor to match any proposed repair to the correct OEM troubleshooting tree and part number.
